Food presets Brands Chart Guide EN English Español Português Français Deutsch Why convection recipes need their own conversion A convection oven and an air fryer work on the same principle: a fan pushes hot air around the food so heat reaches it faster than it would in still air. That means a recipe written for convection already has most of the air fryer's advantage built in — it is usually set about 25°F lower than the conventional-oven version of the same dish, and often runs a little shorter. Put that recipe through a standard oven-to-air-fryer conversion and you take the 25°F off a second time, which is how fan-oven recipes come out of an air fryer basket pale and underdone. This converter starts from the convection number and applies only the gap that is actually left. Why the cut is smaller What remains between a convection oven and an air fryer is size and distance. An air fryer's cavity is a fraction of the volume, and the food sits a few inches from both the fan and the heating element, so the air reaches it faster and the surface browns sooner. That is worth roughly 0–15°F and 5–10% of the time, depending on the food. Fries and wings keep almost all of their heat — they need it to crisp and render fat — and save time instead. Baked goods and casseroles take the biggest temperature cut, 15°F, because in a small cavity the top browns before the center sets. Oven-style air fryers are closer still to a convection oven, so their cut shrinks by another 5°F. Worked example A fan-oven recipe at 350°F for 30 minutes, general food, in a basket air fryer, comes out at 340°F for 27 minutes. Put the same numbers through the conventional oven-to-air-fryer converter and you would get 325°F for 24 minutes — too low and too short for a recipe that was already fan-adjusted. Wings at 425°F convection for 40 minutes run hotter than a 400°F basket can go, so the converter holds them at 400°F and adds time back: 39 minutes, with a note telling you it did. How to tell if a recipe is written for convection Look for the words first: "fan", "fan-forced", "fan oven", "convection bake", "convection roast", or a temperature written as "180°C fan". UK and Australian recipes and food packaging often print two numbers, one conventional and one fan, and the fan one is the lower. If there is no label, compare the temperature with what the dish usually takes: roast potatoes at 400°F rather than 425°F, or cookies at 325°F rather than 350°F, suggest the recipe already assumes a fan. Recipe books that come with an oven are usually written for its convection setting. If the recipe isn't convection A recipe for a standard, fan-off oven needs the full conversion — the larger temperature drop and bigger time cut the oven-to-air-fryer converter applies. Using this page for a conventional recipe leaves food slightly hot and long; using the conventional converter for a convection recipe leaves it underdone. Match the converter to the recipe, not to your appliance. Oven → Air Fryer converter (conventional recipes) → Air Fryer → Convection converter → Air Fryer → Oven converter → Printable conversion chart → Frozen food mode (packaging instructions) → Frequently Asked Questions How do I convert a convection oven recipe to an air fryer? Lower the temperature by 0–15°F depending on the food and cut the time by 5–10%. Crisping foods like fries and wings keep their heat and lose a little time; baked goods and casseroles take the biggest temperature cut. The converter above applies the per-food numbers and checks the result against your air fryer's maximum temperature. Do I subtract 25°F from a convection recipe for the air fryer? No. That 25°F is the usual conventional-to-convection adjustment, and a convection recipe has already made it. Subtracting it again double-counts the fan and leaves food underdone. From convection, the remaining cut is 15°F at most. Is a fan oven the same as a convection oven? Yes. "Fan oven" and "fan-forced" are the UK and Australian names for a convection oven. When packaging lists a conventional and a fan temperature, enter the fan one here. What if the convection recipe is hotter than my air fryer can go? The converter holds the temperature at your unit's ceiling — 400°F for most basket models, 450°F for oven-style units — and adds about 8% of the time back to make up the difference, with a note under the result. Check early; the surface may brown a little less. Can I use convection settings unchanged in an oven-style air fryer? Almost. An oven-style air fryer is essentially a small convection oven, so the cut shrinks: 0–10°F and close to the original time. Fries and wings can run at the convection temperature with only a few minutes off. Do internal temperature targets change between convection and air frying? No. Pull poultry at 165°F internal and fish, steak, or chops at 145°F, whichever appliance you use. The converter changes the setting and time to get there, not what done means.
